title: Handed down (CCC 74–79)
hookLine: the apostles handed on their mission to bishops

cards: "And the things which thou hast heard of me by many witnesses, the same commend to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also." That's Paul, writing to Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims.
Follow the people in that one sentence. Paul speaks. Timothy hears.
Timothy hands it to faithful men. They teach others. And the others, presumably, will teach others again.
It's a relay, written into a single verse. Today's word is that relay, as the Catholic Church understands it: apostolic succession.

teach.b: Day two hundred ninety-three paired scripture and Tradition; today follows the line further. The Catechism calls the handing-on of the faith tradition, a living transmission.

The apostles, it says, handed on what they received in two ways: by word of mouth, in their preaching, example, and the communities and customs they set up; and in writing, in the books that became the New Testament.
Then a third thing. To keep the gospel whole and alive in the Church, the apostles left bishops as their successors, handing over their own teaching role. That's apostolic succession.
Catholic teaching sees today's bishops as successors of the apostles, each ordained by the laying on of hands by bishops before him. An early letter already speaks this way.

A letter from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth, which tradition credits to Clement, says the apostles appointed leaders and made provision that, when those leaders died, other approved men should succeed to their ministry.

Orthodox Christians also hold to the succession of bishops. Other churches understand faithfulness to the apostles in other ways, some by holding to the apostles' teaching in scripture rather than to a line of bishops.
And Catholic teaching adds a limit: the Church's teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it.

teach.h: A LINK IN THE CHAIN, NOT THE SOURCE.
teach.b: The bishop is a link in the chain, not the source of what runs through it.
In the Catholic picture, it's less a family tree of power than a chain of hands, each passing on what it was given, and answerable for passing it on whole.

how: At every Mass, the Eucharistic Prayer names the pope and the local bishop, and bishops are ordained by other bishops through the laying on of hands, which Catholics understand as the succession from the apostles.

games.q: you're one of the apostles, and you won't live forever. how do you make sure the message outlasts you?
o: trust that people will remember it
preach, write, and provide for successors
write it down and leave it at that
games.why: the Catechism says they preached and wrote, and left bishops as their successors; the letter credited to Clement says they provided for others to succeed.

practice: Think of your bishop, by name if you know it, or simply whoever holds that role where you live, and the weight of the job: one person asked to keep an old message whole, in a place full of new problems.
If you pray, say their name and ask God's help for them; if you don't, wish them wisdom plainly, the way you'd wish it for anyone carrying something heavy.

wordCard.voice: Apostolic succession. The bishops as successors of the apostles, a teaching role handed on hand to hand, in service of the word of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an overseer. The New Testament word that Catholic Bibles render as bishop.

carryVoice: Your line: an unbroken line. Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, and on to others also. Until tomorrow.
